#214. Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?

El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible with human rights.

Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.

These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.

More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.

De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.

But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.

According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.

It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.

Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.

Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.

However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).

The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.

"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe.  As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.

Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.

However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.

Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."

Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.

Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.

However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.

In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.

In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.

Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.

Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.

#211. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#209. Amidst fears of AI-cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’

During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.

“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”

In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.

Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”

“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.

“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added, on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure…and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”

Nadella made a broader point, as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.

“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.

“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.

Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.

Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.

Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. #200. Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail

As Nigeria's January 2027 elections approach, political violence and thuggery at campaign rallies and town hall meetings raise concerns about voter safety.

Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering.

"I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.

Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.

During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."

He was left in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.

As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.

Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja.

Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.

Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation.

On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwaso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.

Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.

Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria.

Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."

Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.

"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.

A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."

Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority.

However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.

"Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.

Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more to the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

#199. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#196. Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban

The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways

Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.

A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.

Waymo’s voluntary suspension came the same day as the California department of motor vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from the state’s freeways. The ban followed two traffic incidents, including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, a DMV spokesperson, Jonathan Groveman, said in a statement.

The construction zone incident occurred on 5 November, and the second incident, which involved California highway patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.

Video of the 6 November incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.

“The department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.

Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on 18 May.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”.

California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on the state’s freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”.

#192. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

In addition to Jenrick, the former home secretary Suella Braverman, the former DWP shadow minister Danny Kruger and the former Foreign Office shadow minister Andrew Rosindell are among the Tory MPs to have defected to Reform.

Yusuf qualified his comments by saying Braverman and Jenrick had either been sacked or resigned “over immigration policy or issues around culture”. The comments raise questions about unity at the top of Reform.

Braverman, Reform’s education spokesperson, and Jenrick have waded into immigration and cultural issues since joining Reform. The claims that former Tories have no role in immigration policy for Reform also appear to be at odds with, for example, Jenrick’s announcement in June of plans for a levy on migrant labour.

Reform’s grassroots members have long appeared suspicious of former Conservatives in their midst. Farage himself has frequently had to push back against claims that his party had become “the Conservative party 2.0” and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections were held on 7 May. Jenrick and others who defected nonetheless maintain a strong influence within Reform.

Tom Milford, a former spokesperson for Jenrick, has become Reform’s head of press, while the MP himself continues to generate slickly produced videos for social media covering a range of topics including law and order.

Jenrick is often mooted alongside Yusuf and Richard Tice as the most likely successor to Farage if he was to stand down.

The Labour party said Yusuf had “admitted that most Reform MPs can’t be trusted on their migration policies”.

Anna Turley, the Labour MP and minister of state for border security and asylum, said: “They don’t trust two-thirds of their MPs to work on their immigration policies, yet they expect the country to trust them to secure Britain’s borders.”

#188. ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know

The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague.

The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.

Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.

A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.

"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]… International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.

"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.

In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.

Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.

Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.

The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.

As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.

"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.

Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.

Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.

The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.

"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.

"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.

O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.

Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State, they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.

"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.

"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.

"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.

The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.

The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.

What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.

Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.

Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.

"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

#182. Shabana Mahmood backs ban on police marching in pride events in uniform

Home secretary says ‘routine two-tier policing’ does not exist, but public trust in impartial law enforcement must be restored

Shabana Mahmood has backed a ban on police officers marching in pride events in uniform as she said there had been a “few examples” of two-tier policing.

Although she said there was no systematic or routine two-tier policing, the home secretary said “a new impartiality standard” was necessary to reverse the fall in the public’s faith in law enforcement.

She said one example had been when police officers took part in a pride event in Northumbria last year, which a court found had breached a duty of impartiality. Mahmood said: “The judgment found that they got the balance wrong … and that marching … was not acceptable and not impartial.

“Today at those marches, you will often have campaigners, on gender identity … and those issues are now contested … the marching alongside looks like a political act.”

Nik Adams, the deputy commissioner of City of London police who is also the LGBTQ+ lead for police chiefs, said: “Using the language about LGBTQ issues being contested makes LGBTQ people in policing and wider society feel less safe, makes their lives feel less valued.

“LGBTQ is a protected characteristic in law. The rights are hard won.”

Wiltshire police faces a court challenge next week for setting up a stall at a pride event in Swindon after claims it had exposed a lack of neutrality amid disputes over transgender rights.

Asked if she was accepting there was two-tier policing, Mahmood said: “There’s no systematic, systemic, routine two-tier policing in this country. I reject that charge.

“What Reform and others will have you believe is every single day officers go out and they practise a thing called two-tier policing. That is utter, complete, ridiculous rubbish.

“But there have been examples of differential treatment, and those have had an impact on confidence in policing, and they’ve allowed that false perception of two-tier policing to take hold.

“I accept that there are few examples, and I know that actually the best way to deal with that is to make sure we have a new impartiality standard.”

One police leader told the Guardian this rhetoric was concerning as forces tried to navigate the culture wars buffeting Britain while serving all communities.

She said police had to improve its record on recruiting more black officers, noting there were barely any more than there had been 30 years ago.

Mahmood added: “We must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment. I believe we see this in examples like the old police anti-racism commitment, which was a well-intentioned attempt to address racism that ended up achieving the opposite of its stated goal.

“It made statements that are clearly wrong: to the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing ‘does not mean treating everyone the same’. So was the document’s guidance that officers should not be ‘colour blind’.”

The home secretary also said officers should engage with the community to discuss local issues, but not with activist groups and campaigners who were pushing their own political agenda.

But one source said Mahmood’s soundbites did not take account of the complexities: “It’s an easy slogan, but dig into the details and it becomes more complicated.”

For instance some oppose the red poppy as part of Remembrance Day celebrations, believing it glorifies militarism, but these are worn by officers and chiefs.

Mahmood decried police talking to activists, but policing has been given money to boost the protection of Jewish people in Britain, while some groups that police may want to consult have been accused of extremism by pro-Palestinian groups.

Gavin Stephens, the chair of the National Police Chiefs Council, said: “Public trust depends on the police being seen to act fairly and impartially. Barriers to justice remain, discrimination still exists within our own ranks, and we rely on the trust and confidence of all communities to do our job. A diverse service is a stronger service.”

#181. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#178. Birmingham council granted interim ban on union jacks on lamp-posts

High court judge issues order against Raise the Colours over flags on council-owned street furniture

The campaign group Raise the Colours has been temporarily banned from placing union jacks on lamp-posts and roundabouts in Birmingham after a legal challenge by the local council.

The high court judge Emma Kelly granted an interim injunction banning the placing of all flags on council-owned street furniture without prior permission in a judgment issued on Wednesday, Birmingham city council said.

The council, run by a minority coalition led by the Liberal Democrats, sought the injunction against seven people identified as supporting or participating in the affixing of flags in the city, including Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of Raise the Colours, and “persons unknown”.

The application for an injunction, which attracted national attention and follows similar action by Oxfordshire county council, argued the actions of the flag activists had caused danger, alarm and distress.

People associated with Raise the Colours, which describes itself as a grassroots movement, have been placing union jacks and St George’s flags on public infrastructure across the country since August last year.

The group’s website states it is a “campaign to cover Britain in symbols of unity and patriotism”. However, others have accused the group of racism and spreading anti-immigration rhetoric – claims it has previously denied.

In its claim to the high court, Birmingham city council said the defendants had travelled across the city “unlawfully affixing flags” and had confronted residents who attempted to remove them.

“In doing so, they are engaging in tortious and criminal behaviour, which is both antisocial and dangerous,” the claim read, adding that the behaviour had caused “danger” and “alarm” to residents.

The council said residents of Birmingham had suffered “fear, anxiety, intimidation, harassment,” been put at “serious risk of harm”, and some had suffered physical injuries, including a broken leg.

The case was adjourned in early September after the judge said she was “troubled by the lack of clarity” from the council “against the individual defendants”, and a further hearing was scheduled at the end of September.

Bridge opposed the injunction and read a written statement to the court. He said: “For me, the union flag represents home, identity, belonging, national identity, British culture and patriotism.”

His lawyer, Liam Wells, argued that the injunction would have a “chilling effect” on human rights and that erecting union jacks and St George’s flags was an expression of his political views.

Wells said the interim injunction would risk “silencing people in their political views and expression of political opinions” and the council had failed to prove Bridge had acted unlawfully.

Three local residents, Adam Biggs, Mark Hudson and Tony Kaye, joined the case representing ‘persons unknown’ opposing the injunction bid, and expressed concerns it would ban people flying flags for pride and other campaigns.

The council’s cabinet member for equalities, communities and social justice, Jane Baston, said on Wednesday the local authority was grateful for the judgment and it was an “important step”.

“We have taken a proportionate and evidence-led approach throughout this case. Our priority has always been to protect public safety, supporting the welfare of our staff and contractors, maintaining community cohesion and ensuring public funds are used responsibly,” she said.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

In a video uploaded to Facebook, Bridge said he was “gutted” and “devastated” by the decision, including the fact that the injunction granted power of arrest against him and others.

He said Raise the Colours was “not about race, colour, creed” but about opposing “illegal invaders breaking in our country, jeopardising our borders, on the rubber dinghies”.

At the Reform UK conference in Birmingham in September, Nigel Farage promised to help Bridge in his legal fight if the party was able to do so.

In response to the judgment, Reform’s leader in Birmingham, Jex Parkin, said the council had its “priorities entirely wrong” and had pursued an “ideologically driven case against residents proudly displaying our national flags – at huge public expense”.

The leader of the local Conservatives, Robert Alden, also criticised the injunction and said the council was “punishing ordinary Birmingham residents who simply want to show pride in where they live”.

He said: “Amidst a 23-month bin strike, loss of roads funding, and mounting litter on our streets, the council has chosen to make this court action a priority.”

The group Brummies United Against Racism, which campaigned for the injunction, welcomed the judgment. Members of the group told the Guardian earlier this year they had presented evidence of incidents involving Raise the Colours to the police and council officers.

The group said it was “not opposed to this country’s flag” and many of its supporters “see the flag as a symbol of celebration and unity”. “However, we are firmly opposed to those who seek to use the flag to further an agenda of hate and who dress up racism as patriotism,” a statement read.

A further hearing in the case will take place on Thursday.

#177. India: Online censorship grows after 'Cockroach' protests

Since anti-government Cockroach protests erupted, journalists and creators say their content is increasingly being restricted on social media in India.

A video showing a young girl crying as she spoke about alleged police brutality during the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in July. A video examining the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's (RSS) contribution to the rise of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). A satirical cartoon criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

These are among the examples of content that have recently been restricted on social media in India.

Content creator CitySavitri describes herself as a "nobody" in the world of social media. She had started making videos just two months ago and had around 600 followers on Instagram.

Yet a video looking at the RSS's role in the BJP's 2014 election victory was restricted in India within an hour of being posted. It was the first of three videos she posted that faced restrictions.

The experience made her feel that "anti-government commentary" was being monitored and curtailed.

"It is very plain and simple to understand," the content creator told DW.

Independent journalist Sadhika Tiwari was covering the CJP protest in New Delhi on July 20, when police used batons and tear gas against demonstrators.

Tiwari's video of a frightened young girl crying and speaking about police brutality garnered around 10 million views within hours, she said, before it was restricted in India.

Political cartoonist Satish Acharya has also faced repeated restrictions, with Instagram blocking his profile twice recently.

In May 2025, during the conflict between India and Pakistan, independent digital news outlet Maktoob Media's X account was withheld in India while it was reporting on the escalating crisis, its founder and editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told DW.

"We received no official notice or email from either the government or X. It was our readers who first alerted us to the blocking," he said.

Maktoob Media said it contacted Indian officials and X but received no response. Access to the account was restored a few days later, again without an explanation.

Kayyalakkath said Maktoob's content from the July protest also faced restrictions. "Suppressing independent journalism undermines transparency, accountability and democratic values," he said.

Several of the content creators and journalists interviewed by DW said they received no prior notification or explanation for the restrictions.

Some users were not sure if their content had been blocked at the government's request or proactively by the social media platforms.

When asked for comment, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, pointed DW to a website statement noting users can appeal content and account restrictions.

At the heart of the debate are India's IT Rules, 2021, amended in February 2026. Section 79 of India's IT Act protects social media platforms and other intermediaries from liability for content posted by third parties, provided they meet certain legal conditions.

One such requirement, introduced through the February 2026 amendments, is to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content within three hours of receiving a valid court order or a reasoned government notice. The previous deadline was 36 hours.

Failure to comply can result in intermediaries losing their liability protection.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The government's Sahyog portal, which coordinates takedown requests between law enforcement, platforms and telecom providers, has faced criticism over the pace at which notices are issued.

Meta said it uses automated tools and technologies to detect and review content that may violate its community standards. It also automatically restricts access to certain types of content in India to comply with legal requirements under the IT rules.

Pranesh Prakash, a technology law and policy adviser, said the amended rules allow authorized police officials to notify intermediaries about content they consider unlawful without necessarily filing a formal complaint or initiating other legal proceedings.

"This has led to the worst period of social media censorship that India has ever seen, with digital news media accounts being blocked, cartoonists' accounts being blocked, and even mere discussions of an opposition leader's memoirs being blocked," he said. "Clearly, none of these disclosed any 'unlawful acts.'"

Prakash also raised concerns about the lack of public information on government requests to remove content, saying this made it difficult to assess the scale of restrictions.

The Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in), a digital rights organization, said the growing reliance on automated takedowns raised serious concerns about transparency, accountability and due process.

"There is little transparency about the processes through which content is identified, flagged and restricted, or whether there is any meaningful human oversight before a takedown is implemented," SFLC.in told DW.

The organization also tested X's verification process by submitting a takedown request against one of its own posts using a fake email address. X registered the request, raising questions about how it verified the identity and authority of those submitting requests.

After SFLC.in alerted the company, X introduced email verification codes for people submitting takedown requests.

"A channel that lets anyone pose as a law enforcement official can be misused to silence lawful speech," SFLC.in said.

X did not respond to DW's request for a comment.

The Indian government denies that it is censoring online content.

While the ministry did not respond to DW's latest request for a comment, in an email response to DW in August, Vinod Kumar, chief of media and communications at the Information Technology Ministry, said Instagram posts by students and protesters following the July CJP protests "are not being taken down as alleged."

"Media enjoys freedom in India. The Government does not censor online content," Kumar said, adding that the government only acts against "objectionable content."

Under the Indian IT rules, "unlawful content" generally refers to material which could threaten India's sovereignty and integrity, disturb public order, incite violence, or constitute defamation.

However, social media influencers such as university professor Madri Kakoti, alias Dr. Medusa, continue to report restrictions. Kakoti's Instagram account was restricted in India on November 16 without notice, she said, along with that of satirist Shamita Yadav.

Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have warned that expanding content restrictions could chill free expression and encourage self-censorship among journalists, creators and ordinary users.

Acharya, however, said he would continue his work.

"The Indian Constitution gives me the right to draw political cartoons," he said. "It's totally democratic to question and criticize the government in India."

For Tiwari, the issue goes beyond the reach of a single video. It is also about preserving a record of what happened, after the Delhi Police denied allegations of using excessive force during the July 20 protest in front of the Supreme Court.

"We have seen several other videos now, and it's well established why that girl was crying, and that the Delhi Police used force and lied about it," she said.

"Still, I want that video back up because it needs to stay for posterity. I think that's the larger idea: they want to take this stuff down so it fades from memory, allowing them to categorically deny it later when we have little left to show for what happened."

Raise the Colours activist Billy Allison, 36, killed man in ‘completely unprovoked and unjustified’ attack, say police

A member of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has been found guilty of murdering a man in a “completely unprovoked and unjustified” attack.

Billy Allison, 36, delivered a “very, very hard” punch with the “stance and skill of an experienced fighter” which killed 44-year-old Matthew O’Gara while he was on a night out in Lichfield on 24 May.

A jury of seven men and five women were not told of Allison’s link to Raise the Colours, which has been responsible for hanging hundreds of union jack flags on lamp-posts and roundabouts across the country, during the trial at Stafford crown court.

Allison was also found guilty of grievous bodily harm with intent on Wednesday for twice punching O’Gara’s friend, 62-year-old Adam Cooper, on the same night as the murder, leaving him with a fractured eye socket and nose.

O’Gara’s family thanked the emergency services who cared for him and said he remained “deeply loved” and “will always hold a special place in our hearts”.

“While the conclusion of the court proceedings has brought a measure of justice, it can never replace the loss we have suffered or bring Matthew back,” they said in a statement.

The trial heard how Allison had been drinking and had taken cocaine before he attacked the two men – neither of whom he knew.

He had spent the day with his partner, Charlotte Dean, and fellow Raise the Colours members Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen and their partners.

CCTV images capturing the lead-up to the assault showed Allison in the corner of the dancefloor alongside Bridge at about 11.30pm.

Prosecution counsel Timothy Hannam described how Allison, without warning, then took three “purposeful” steps toward an “oblivious” O’Gara and delivered a “very, very hard punch” causing him to fall to the floor and become “motionless”.

The punch was “hard enough to break several bones” in O’Gara’s neck, Hannam said, and caused a massive brain haemorrhage which resulted in the 44-year-old going into cardiac arrest. He died in hospital two days later.

Allison, who had participated in and won boxing competitions, then delivered two “powerful boxer punches” to Cooper’s face. “In total, three devastating punches had been delivered in about six seconds,” Hannam said, adding that the two men had been “demolished by them”.

O’Gara’s partner, Rebecca Mullally, gave evidence during the trial and said O’Gara and their friends were in a “good mood” before the assault.

She said she heard Allison’s punch because it was “really loud” and she did not see “anybody provoke anyone” before the attack.

“I‘ve never seen a punch like that before,” she said. “I did think: ‘Has that killed him?’ It was hard.”

Cooper also gave evidence during the trial and said he felt an “almighty blow to my face” when he was punched by Allison, likening it to a “sledgehammer”.

“I didn’t know it was coming [and] I made no attempt to defend myself,” he said, before describing how blood then poured out of his face.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

After the attack, Allison fled the bar via a back entrance with Cullen and the pair swapped T-shirts. Allison was later found by police at the Cathedral Hotel in Beacon Street at 5am, where Cullen had booked to stay the night. He later answered “no comment” during police questioning.

Police body-worn camera footage showed Allison being told his victim had died and he was facing a murder charge. Allison could be heard muttering “fuck” and “fuck’s sake”.

In his evidence to the court, Allison said he was “really sorry” for what he had done and “really sorry my actions caused the end of someone’s life”.

He said he had never intended to cause anyone really serious injury or death, but accepted O’Gara and Cooper had not done anything to provoke the attack.

Allison added: “I just don’t have an explanation for why … I had a bit of a sense I was being looked at, in my drunken state, maybe I was a touch paranoid.

“I didn’t intentionally punch him that hard.”

DI Lisa Holland, who led the investigation, said: “Matthew O’Gara’s family have been left devastated by his death and our thoughts remain firmly with them.

“This was a wholly unprovoked attack carried out by Allison on a man he did not know and who posed no threat to him. In a matter of seconds, Allison’s actions changed the lives of Matthew’s loved ones for ever.

“The evidence in this case showed that Allison approached Matthew without warning and struck him, causing catastrophic injuries from which he never recovered. He then went on to seriously assault another man.”

Allison, who is facing a mandatory life sentence, has been remanded ahead of his sentencing at Stafford crown court on 5 January.
